title: Getting Started
body: Ledgdex is a simple market on a dex. A dex is a website that dexweb makes from your own files.
A ledgdex is a dex with one more file: a signed ledger that only grows (ledgdex.jsonl). Each seller and each buyer keeps a ledgdex.
A trade then has three records:
- the claim that the buyer signs
- the record of the claim that the seller signs
- the copy of that record that the buyer keeps
Ledgdex needs no server and no blockchain. It uses SHA-256, Ed25519 and plain files. Dex is the core. Dex + ledger is a ledgdex.
These docs are a ledgdex too. Their own ledger has one signature, as a demonstration. Ledgdex makes pages from this ledger. These pages are in the list of pages, next to the written pages.

1. Install ledgdex. You need Python 3.8 or later, and git. For more ways to install, see Installation: 
pip install "ledgdex @ git+https://github.com/ledgdex/ledgdex@v1.0.18#subdirectory=py"

2. Make your ledgdex. This command makes a dex with a new ledger. It keeps a new key in ~/.ledgdex: 
ledgdex init biobot --name "biobot" --key biobot

3. Offer something. Write each price as an integer in the smallest unit of the currency. For example, 250000 is USD 2,500.00: 
cat > offer.json <<EOF
{"item": {"title": "Penjointu v1 weights"}, "quantity": 10, "unit": "license",
 "currency": "USD", "price": 250000, "pay": [{"method": "card", "to": "https://pay.example/biobot"}]}
EOF
ledgdex offer biobot offer.json
4. Open shop/gen/index.html. This is your dex. It has a page for your ledger and a page for the offer. Put your own pages in shop/data.json or shop/to_add/, as in any dex.
5. Publish your ledgdex (Publishing a Ledgdex Online). Buyers then claim from it (Buying). Example: First Trade runs a full trade on one computer.
Where to go next:
- Users who start a market: Set Up a Marketplace.
- Developers: Extending Ledgdex and the API Reference.
- Bots and agents: Bots and Agents.
- All commands: Command Line Options. All examples: Examples.

title: Dex and Ledgdex
body: The dex is the core. A dex is a website that dexweb builds from a folder. The folder holds these items:
- data.json: the pages of the dex.
- config.json: the look of the site, and where dexweb publishes it.
- to_add/: files that dexweb makes into pages.
- gen/: the website.
A dex works alone. You can share it freely. People and bots can read it. Any host for static files can serve it (dex hosting).
Dex + ledger = ledgdex. A ledgdex is a dex with one more file, ledgdex.jsonl. This file is a ledger. Its owner signs each entry, and each entry holds the hash of the entry before it.

Ledgdex reads the ledger and replays it into a state: offers, claims, payments, disputes, auctions, admissions and listings. Then ledgdex writes pages for the state into the same data.json, next to your own pages.
Dexweb builds the site as usual. Nothing else changes: the folder, the build and the hosting stay the same.

dex          = data.json + config.json + to_add/        ->  gen/ (website)
ledgdex      = dex + ledgdex.jsonl (signed ledger)      ->  gen/ (website + ledger pages + ledger)
a market     = many ledgdexes that read each other's ledgers
So all that you know about dexes stays true: dexweb's getting started, its styles and themes, and publishing with python run.py.

Ledgdex adds the commands that sign and record (Command Line Options). Ledgdex also refuses to publish a ledger that does not extend the published ledger. The setting "append_only": ["ledgdex.jsonl"] in config.json does this.
Use a dex when you only publish: documents, a shop window or a journal. Use a ledgdex when people must trust what you publish at a later time.
Examples are offers that people buy from, records of who bought what, and admissions to a market.
You can change a dex into a ledgdex at any time. Run ledgdex init on the dex folder. It keeps the pages and config.json, and it adds a ledger.

This documentation is a dex and a ledgdex. The written pages are the dex. Ledgdex makes three pages from the ledger of the docs: Ledgdex Docs ledger, Example offer: Penjointu v1 weights and Example auction: Penjointu v2 early access.

Load that ledger in the viewer, or check it: 
ledgdex verify https://ledgdex.github.io/docs

title: Installation
body: Ledgdex needs Python 3.8 or later, and dexweb. Pip installs dexweb with ledgdex. To publish to a git repository, for example on GitHub Pages, you also need git. To publish into a folder, you do not need git (Publishing a Ledgdex Online).

1. Install from the release. This is the recommended way: 
pip install "ledgdex @ git+https://github.com/ledgdex/ledgdex@v1.0.18#subdirectory=py"

2. Install with fast, constant-time signing. Use this way on each computer that signs. Without it, ledgdex shows a warning: 
pip install "ledgdex[fast] @ git+https://github.com/ledgdex/ledgdex@v1.0.18#subdirectory=py"

3. Install from a clone, to work on ledgdex itself: 
git clone https://github.com/ledgdex/ledgdex
cd ledgdex
pip install -e "py[fast]"
cd py && python -m unittest discover -s tests

4. Make sure that ledgdex works: 
ledgdex --help
ledgdex verify https://ledgdex.github.io/docs
You do not install the JavaScript core. It is plain ES modules in js/. The site also serves these modules next to the viewer. See JavaScript Core and the API Reference.
Ledgdex keeps keys in ~/.ledgdex, or in $LEDGDEX_HOME when you set it. It keeps the verification cache in ~/.cache/ledgdex, or in $LEDGDEX_CACHE. See Configuration.

title: Ledgdex Directory Structure
body: This list shows the files that ledgdex init shop ... makes. Nothing in the folder is secret. Keys are never in a dex.

shop/
  ledgdex.jsonl        the ledger: a header line and one signed entry for each line (it only grows)
  data.json            the dex pages: your pages, and the pages that ledgdex writes (they start with <!-- ledgdex -->)
  config.json          dexweb settings, "publish" (with "append_only": ["ledgdex.jsonl"]) and "ledgdex"
  styles.css           the look of the site (the ledgdex default: ruled rows, like a ledger)
  run.py               "python run.py" builds the dex with dexweb, as in any dex
  to_add/              files that dexweb adds as pages
  backup/              the dexweb backup of data.json
  gen/                 the website: the published files, with gen/ledgdex.jsonl
  .ledgdex-root.jsonl  the last copy of the root that ledgdex read (only with a root, never published)
  .ledgdex.lock        lets one writer change the dex at a time
  .publish/            the dexweb copy of the repository that it publishes to (only with the git method)

~/.ledgdex/            secret keys, mode 600 (NAME.key), and secret bids until their reveal (bids/)
~/.cache/ledgdex/      a record of the ledger bytes that ledgdex verified before (for speed only)
Ledgdex publishes only gen/. The command ledgdex render shop writes the generated pages again and builds gen/ again. Each command that records an entry does this for you.

title: Set Up a Marketplace
body: A market can serve a place, a trade or a community. It has no platform in the middle. Each member keeps their own ledgdex.
One operator keeps a ledger that has two jobs:
- The index: the list of shops in the market.
- The root: the list of members that the operator admits.
Shops sell to admitted members. Buyers find offers through the index. The operator is the default arbiter of disputes. Example: Marketplace does all of these steps on one computer.

1. The operator makes the ledgdex of the exchange and publishes it (Publishing a Ledgdex Online): 
ledgdex init exchange --name "ONITO medmodel exchange" --about "Trained medical models, from bots to clinics" \
    --key exchange --url https://exchange.example --dest git@github.com:YOU/exchange.git --branch main
ledgdex publish exchange

2. Each seller makes its own ledgdex under the exchange: 
ledgdex init biobot --name "biobot" --key biobot --root https://exchange.example
3. Shops and buyers send their public key to the operator. The commands ledgdex keygen NAME and ledgdex init show the public key.

4. The operator checks who they are, outside the ledger. Then the operator admits them: 
ledgdex admit exchange ed25519:SELLER_KEY --name "biobot"
ledgdex admit exchange ed25519:BUYER_KEY --name "orthonalyzebot"
ledgdex publish exchange

5. The operator lists the sellers: 
ledgdex list exchange https://biobot.example --note "knee bone density models"

6. A seller can offer to admitted members only, with "allow": "admitted". The seller then also admits the buyers that it serves, with ledgdex admit biobot KEY. A seller can also offer to anyone, with "any".

7. Buyers read the index to find offers: 
ledgdex discover https://market.example --offers
8. Each day, each member runs ledgdex check on the ledgers that they trade with (Checking for Tampering). The check finds each rewrite, with signed proof.
The operator decides who is a member and decides disputes. The operator signs these decisions, and anyone can read them.
The operator cannot change the ledger of a member, hide a sale or set a price. The operator's key is the most valuable key in the market.
Keep the operator key offline, and use a device key each day (Keys, Devices and Recovery).
Other ways to run a market:
- Without --root, a market is only an index. Anyone can be in its list.
- Many markets can list the same shop.
- A shop with no root is the arbiter of its own offers, unless it names an arbiter (Disputes and Arbiters).

title: Selling
body: A seller signs offers into its own ledger. The seller records the claims that buyers send, and it records payment and delivery.
1. Write the offer as JSON. These fields are necessary: item.title, quantity, currency and price. The other fields have these default values:

unit         "unit"
allow        "any"
pay          []
terms        ""
item.text    ""
item.media   []
arbiter      the owner of the root, or the seller when the dex names no root

An offer with all fields: 
{"item": {"title": "Penjointu v1 weights", "text": "Weights (SHA256 hash): sha256:...",
          "media": [{"url": "https://biobot.example/model-card.png", "hash": "sha256:..."}]},
 "quantity": 10, "unit": "license", "currency": "USD", "price": 250000,
 "allow": "any", "pay": [{"method": "card", "to": "https://pay.example/biobot"}],
 "terms": "One license for each clinic. Delivered in 2 days.", "expires": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z"}

2. Sign the offer and record it: 
ledgdex offer shop offer.json

3. Collect the claims. They come from the published dex of each buyer, or from files that buyers send to you: 
ledgdex record shop --from https://asha.example --from https://ravi.example
ledgdex record shop claim-1a2b3c4d5e6f.json

4. Record the money when it arrives. Record the delivery when you deliver: 
ledgdex received shop CLAIM_ID 240000
ledgdex delivered shop CLAIM_ID --note "by courier"

5. To stop selling, withdraw the offer: 
ledgdex withdraw shop OFFER_ID

6. Publish after each step that others must see: 
ledgdex publish shop
The state applies these rules to each claim. Anyone can calculate the state again. A claim must obey all of these rules:
- It names the offer by its id and by its hash. So the offer cannot change under the claim.
- It pays the price of the offer.
- It asks for 1 unit or more, and not more than the units that remain.
- It comes from a key that allow admits.
- It arrives before expires.
- It does not come from the seller.
If a claim breaks a rule, the ledger keeps the claim, and the state marks it as rejected, with the reason. If two claims ask for the last unit, the claim that the seller records first wins.
An offer links its media. It never includes the media. Each link has the URL and the SHA-256 of the file. If a picture changes after a sale, ledgdex check --media finds the change.
Prices are integers in the smallest unit of the currency:
- USD and EUR: cents (2 digits).
- JPY: yen.
- BTC: satoshi.
All currency codes work. The pages format the codes that they know. See A Trade, Step by Step and Example: First Trade.

title: Buying
body: A buyer signs claims, payments and confirmations with its own key. It keeps a copy of each message as sent in its own ledger. When you publish your dex, you send these messages.
To buy, you need your own ledgdex (ledgdex init orthonalyzebot --name "orthonalyzebot" --key orthonalyzebot), or only a browser (The Viewer).
1. Find the offer on the dex of the seller, or through an index (Indexes and Discovery).

2. Claim the offer. Ledgdex reads the ledger of the seller. If the offer is open, ledgdex signs the exact hash and price of the offer: 
ledgdex claim orthonalyzebot https://biobot.example OFFER_ID --quantity 2
3. Send the claim. Publish your dex (ledgdex publish me). The seller then collects the claim with ledgdex record shop --from https://asha.example.
You can also send the file claim-....json in any way.

4. Keep the receipts. A receipt is the seller's signed record of your message: 
ledgdex receipt orthonalyzebot https://biobot.example

5. Pay as the offer tells you, outside the ledger. Then tell the seller that you paid. When the goods arrive, tell the seller with confirm: 
ledgdex pay orthonalyzebot https://biobot.example CLAIM_ID --method card --ref PAY-0001
ledgdex confirm orthonalyzebot https://biobot.example CLAIM_ID
6. If a problem occurs, see Disputes and Arbiters.
Your receipts are your proof. A receipt is an entry, with the signature of the seller, that records your claim at a position in the ledger of the seller.
If the seller rewrites its ledger at a later time, ledgdex check on your ledger shows the rewrite (Tampering).

title: A Trade, Step by Step
body: This table shows who signs each message, which ledgers keep it, and the status of the claim after each step. Example: First Trade runs these steps.

step                         signed by   kept in                     claim status
offer                        seller      seller ledger               (offer open)
claim                        buyer       buyer (sent), seller        accepted, or rejected with a reason
receipt of the claim         buyer       buyer ledger                (the third entry)
paid                         buyer       buyer (sent), seller        accepted, paid
received                     seller      seller ledger               accepted, received
delivered                    seller      seller ledger               accepted, delivered
confirmed                    buyer       buyer (sent), seller        closed (once received + delivered + confirmed)
dispute                      either      seller ledger               disputed
ruling                       arbiter     seller ledger               released, refunded or split
The state tests the rejection reasons in this order: unknown_offer, offer_changed, withdrawn, expired, self_claim, not_allowed, bad_quantity, price_mismatch.
Some messages break no structure rule, but no state rule accepts them. Examples are a payment from a different key, a ruling by the wrong key, and a message that the seller records two times.
The ledger keeps these messages. The state lists them in ignored, with a reason. They never break the ledger.

To read the state of a ledger: 
ledgdex state https://biobot.example
ledgdex state biobot | python3 -m json.tool

title: Disputes and Arbiters
body: Each offer and each auction names an arbiter. The arbiter is a key that can decide disputes about the offer. The seller signs the arbiter into the offer, so buyers see it before they buy.
The default arbiter is the owner of the root when the dex names a root. In other cases, the default arbiter is the seller.
To name a different arbiter, add this field to the offer: "arbiter": {"key": "ed25519:...", "url": "https://assoc.example"}.

1. The buyer or the seller opens a dispute about an accepted claim, with evidence: 
ledgdex dispute orthonalyzebot CLAIM_ID --seller https://biobot.example --text "No weights came." --evidence PAY-0001
2. The seller records the dispute (ledgdex record shop --from https://asha.example). The status of the claim is then disputed.

3. The arbiter rules, from its own ledgdex: 
ledgdex ruling exchange https://biobot.example DISPUTE_ID --outcome refund --text "No proof of delivery."
4. The seller records the ruling. The status of the claim becomes released, refunded or split.
If a different key rules, the ledger keeps the ruling, and the state ignores it (not_arbiter). The arbiter can decide a dispute one time only.
Money moves outside the ledger. A ruling is a signed decision. The parties and their market do what it says.
Example: Disputes runs these steps. In this example, a seller also tries to decide its own dispute.

title: Sealed-Bid Auctions
body: An auction accepts secret bids until close. A bid signs only a hash of the amount and a random nonce. So nobody can see the amount, not even the seller.
After close, each bidder reveals the amount. After reveal_until, the best valid reveal wins, by rule.

{"item": {"title": "Penjointu v2 early access"}, "currency": "USD",
 "close": "2026-11-01T12:00:00Z", "reveal_until": "2026-11-02T12:00:00Z",
 "best": "highest", "reserve": 1000000}

1. The seller starts the auction: 
ledgdex auction biobot auction.json

2. Bidders bid. The amount and the nonce stay in ~/.ledgdex/bids until the reveal: 
ledgdex bid orthonalyzebot https://biobot.example AUCTION_ID --amount 1350000

3. After close, each bidder reveals: 
ledgdex reveal orthonalyzebot https://biobot.example AUCTION_ID
4. The seller records bids and reveals when they arrive (ledgdex record).
5. After reveal_until, the state names the winner, and the status is awarded. The trade then continues as a claim: paid, delivered, confirmed.
The rules:
- Each key can bid one time.
- The state ignores bids after close, and reveals outside the reveal time.
- A reveal must match its bid.
- With "best": "lowest", the auction is a procurement. The lowest amount at or below reserve wins.
- If two bids tie, the earlier bid wins.
The state judges a ledger at its last entry. So, to announce the result, the seller adds an entry after reveal_until, for example a note. See Example: Auction.

title: Keys, Devices and Recovery
body: A self is its owner key: an Ed25519 key in ~/.ledgdex/NAME.key. The file has mode 600. Ledgdex refuses a key file that other users can read.
The owner key signs messages to other ledgers. It also signs the types that only the owner can sign: device, device_revoke, rotate, and recover in a root.

A device key lets a phone, a till or a robot sign everyday entries without the owner key. Examples are offers, records and deliveries: 
PUB=$(ledgdex keygen phone)        # on the phone
ledgdex device add shop "$PUB" --name "shop phone"   # with the owner key
ledgdex device revoke shop "$PUB" --reason lost
A revoked device cannot sign more entries. The entries that it signed before stay valid.
Give device keys only to devices that you trust with the ledger. A revoke cannot undo what a stolen device could sign while it was active.
To replace the owner key, rotate it. The old key signs the rotation: ledgdex rotate biobot --key biobot-2027.
If the owner loses the owner key, use recovery:
1. The root operator checks who the owner is.
2. The root names a new key for the ledger.
3. The owner gets the ledger again with the new key.

A recovery removes all device keys. 
NEW=$(ledgdex keygen biobot-new)                       # owner, on a new computer
ledgdex recover exchange https://biobot.example "$NEW" # root operator, with the owner key of the root
ledgdex recovered biobot --root https://exchange.example --key biobot-new
Keep a backup of each owner key offline. Example: Keys runs all of these steps.

title: The Root and Admission
body: The root is a ledger with three jobs:
- Its admit and revoke entries tell who is in a market.
- Its recover entries name new keys for lost keys.
- Its owner is the default arbiter.
A dex names its root one time: ledgdex init ... --root https://market.example, or "ledgdex": {"root": ...} in config.json.
Each dex pins its root by the ledger id (root_id). Ledgdex writes root_id the first time it reads the root.
After that, ledgdex refuses a different ledger at that address, and it refuses a broken ledger.
Ledgdex keeps the last copy of the root that it read (.ledgdex-root.jsonl). So the market continues to work when the root's site is down. Ledgdex never accepts an older copy.
"allow": "admitted" means this: the seller's own ledger and the root both admitted the buyer at the time of the claim.

A later revoke never cancels a past sale. To admit and to revoke: 
ledgdex admit exchange ed25519:KEY --name "orthonalyzebot" --note "member since 2026"
ledgdex revoke exchange ed25519:KEY --reason "left the exchange"
A root can belong to a market, a city or The Matrix. To run a root, read Running the root in the README.

title: Indexes and Discovery
body: An index is a ledger that lists other ledgers. Its list and delist entries hold the ledger id, the address, the owner key and a note.
Anyone can run an index. Usually, the index of a market is also its root.

ledgdex list exchange https://biobot.example --note "knee bone density models"
ledgdex delist exchange LEDGER_ID --reason closed
Discovery reads an index. With --offers, it also reads the open offers and auctions of each listed ledger, with their signed price and terms.

With --json, it writes JSON for programs: 
ledgdex discover https://market.example --offers
ledgdex discover https://market.example --offers --json
If a listed address serves a different ledger, discovery reports it and does not trust it. Example: Marketplace and Example: Bots choose offers in this way.

title: Publishing a Ledgdex Online
body: You publish a ledgdex in the same way as any dex, with dexweb. The destination is a git repository or a folder. GitHub Pages hosts git repositories at no cost.
One thing is different: config.json has "append_only": ["ledgdex.jsonl"]. So dexweb refuses to publish a ledger that does not extend the published ledger.
1. Make a repository. On GitHub, use YOU.github.io, or any repository with Pages on.

2. Name the repository when you run init, or at a later time in "publish" in config.json: 
ledgdex init biobot --name "biobot" --key biobot --url https://YOU.github.io \
    --dest git@github.com:YOU/YOU.github.io.git --branch main

3. Publish after each change: 
ledgdex publish shop

4. Others read your ledgdex at its address: 
ledgdex verify https://YOU.github.io
With a git repository, you can publish from many devices. Each device keeps a copy of the dex and has its own device key.
If a different device published first, ledgdex publish signs the unpublished entries of this device again, after the published ledger. Then it publishes again.
So there is one history, and never two entries at one position. Example: Publish runs these steps with a local repository.
Static hosting is enough. Examples are GitHub Pages, any web server, or a shared folder on a local network. Computers can trade over plain HTTP (Bots and Agents).

Publish into a folder, without git. Dexweb has a second publish method, folder. It copies gen/ into a folder. Use it for a dex on your own computer, for tests, or for a web server on a local network. You do not need git or a repository.

1. Make the dex without --dest. The --url is the address where the web server will serve the published dex: 
ledgdex init biobot --name "biobot" --key biobot --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/biobot

2. ledgdex init writes only the settings of the git method. So add "method" and "path" to "publish" in config.json. The path is relative to the dex folder: 
"publish": {"method": "folder", "path": "../site/shop", "append_only": ["ledgdex.jsonl"]}

3. Publish after each change. Dexweb copies gen/ into ../site/shop. The append_only check works as with git: 
ledgdex publish shop

4. Serve the folder site with any web server, for example python3 -m http.server 8000 in that folder. Then others read your ledgdex at its address: 
ledgdex verify http://127.0.0.1:8000/shop

Use the folder method on one device only. It has no atomic step. Thus two devices that publish into one folder at the same time can overwrite each other. With a git repository, ledgdex finds the conflict, catches up and publishes again.

title: Checking for Tampering
body: When a ledger verifies, it is consistent and its owner signed it. But it is not always the history that you saw before. An owner can sign all entries again from a given point.
ledgdex check closes this gap. It compares the ledger with the copies that it saw before, and with the receipts that other selves hold.

ledgdex check biobot orthonalyzebot https://biobot.example   # one time; exit code 1 on tampering
ledgdex check biobot --every 3600                           # as a worker
17 6 * * * cd /srv && ledgdex check biobot --json report.json   # from cron
ledgdex workflow biobot/ledgdex.jsonl > .github/workflows/ledgdex-check.yml   # each day on GitHub
Errors come with signed proof in .ledgdex-check/proofs/:
- equivocation: the ledger is different from the copy that the check saw before.
- receipt_mismatch: a copy has a different entry at the position where a receipt holds a signed entry.
- ledger_changed: an address serves a different ledger.
- broken, media_changed, published_differs.
A warning tells you that the check could not check something: stale, unreachable, needs_root, receipt_bad_signer, receipt_url_mismatch, future_time, media_unavailable, behind.
Check the ledgers that you trade with each day. Example: Check shows how the check finds a rewrite.

title: The Viewer
body: The viewer is a dex too. In a browser, it does what the command line does:
- It loads any ledger by address or from a file.
- It verifies each hash and each signature.
- It shows the ledger as the pages of its dex.
It also keeps your own ledger. It signs claims, payments, confirmations, disputes, bids and reveals, and it collects your receipts.
It downloads your ledger as a complete dex, for you to publish. The viewer uploads nothing.
1. Open a ledger: https://ledgdex.github.io/viewer/index.html?ledger=https://biobot.example.
2. Click New key. Then click Keep, sealed, with a passphrase. The viewer stores the key only in encrypted form. Then click Download key backup.
3. Create your ledger, and sign a claim to the loaded ledger.
4. Click Download your dex, and publish it like any dex. The seller collects your claim from it.
The viewer signs with the Web Crypto Ed25519 of the browser when the browser has it. It refuses to run inside a frame on a different site.
It loads nothing from other sites. For production use, serve the viewer from its own address.

title: Command Line Options
body: Every command and option, generated from ledgdex --help. SELLER, LEDGER and INDEX are a dex address (https://...), a dex folder or a ledgdex.jsonl file; DEX is your own dex folder; ids are sha256: and 64 hex digits; keys are ed25519: and 64 hex digits, or the name of a key in ~/.ledgdex where noted. Messages to another ledger are written to a file (--output, or a name made from the message) and kept as sent in your ledger.

Commands: keygen, init, offer, withdraw, received, delivered, admit, revoke, note, delist, device, record, claim, pay, confirm, receipt, rotate, recover, recovered, dispute, ruling, auction, bid, reveal, list, discover, sign, verify, state, render, check, workflow, publish.
ledgdex keygen

usage: ledgdex keygen [-h] name

make a key in ~/.ledgdex and print its public key

positional arguments:
  name

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
ledgdex init

usage: ledgdex init [-h] --name NAME [--about ABOUT] [--url URL] --key KEY [--dexname DEXNAME] [--dest DEST]
                    [--branch BRANCH] [--site-path SITE_PATH] [--root ROOT]
                    dex

make a ledgdex: a complete dex with a new ledger

positional arguments:
  dex                   the dex folder

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --name NAME           your name, shown on the ledger
  --about ABOUT         one line about you or your shop
  --url URL             this dex's web address
  --key KEY             key name in ~/.ledgdex (made if missing)
  --dexname DEXNAME     dex name (default: --name)
  --dest DEST           repository address to publish to
  --branch BRANCH       branch to publish to
  --site-path SITE_PATH
                        folder in the repository to publish to (default: its root)
  --root ROOT           the root ledger this dex trades under (dex, file or URL): admission, recovery and
                        the default arbiter; pinned by its ledger id
ledgdex offer

usage: ledgdex offer [-h] dex file

sell something: sign and record an offer from a JSON file

positional arguments:
  dex         the dex folder
  file

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
ledgdex withdraw

usage: ledgdex withdraw [-h] dex offer

withdraw an offer

body: Ledgdex is a Python package (ledgdex, in py/) and a JavaScript core (js/) that make the same bytes, ids, signatures and state. Signatures and descriptions below are generated from the code. Start with Example: Python API, Example: JavaScript and Extending Ledgdex; the format is in Ledger File Format and the specification.

class ledgdex.core.Ledger(data, cache=True, root=None)
A parsed ledger. Verification stops at the first structurally invalid line (spec 3.3).

Verified prefixes are cached (in ~/.cache/ledgdex, by ledger id, length and SHA-256 of the exact bytes), so a ledger that only grew is verified only from where it was verified before. Any changed byte misses the cache and is verified in full. cache=False, or LEDGDEX_NO_CACHE=1, always verifies everything.

A receipt verifies on its own (spec 5.1, invariant 10): the entry is signed by the other ledger's header key, or by a key that the key entries in "keys" (rotate, device, device_revoke, recovered, in order) lead to. A "recovered" key entry is checked against the root, as in the ledger itself: without it anyone could hand the other ledger to a key of their own and sign a false receipt.
ledgdex.core.root_recovers(root, ledger_id, e, prior=())

Spec 5.7: a "recovered" entry e of ledger ledger_id is signed by the new key, which a "recover" entry in the root names. A recover entry is spent by its first "recovered" (prior: the ledger's earlier key entries). Nothing the ledger's own keys do can void it: they may be a thief's, and entry times are theirs to choose. Raises Invalid otherwise.

When a claim or bid is judged against the root (spec 5.7), in seconds: the later of the time its author signed it (msg.at, which the seller cannot move) and the time the seller recorded it less the allowed skew (which the buyer cannot move back: a revoked key cannot buy by dating its claim before the revoke). Read a ledger from a dex folder, a file, or a dex URL. Returns (Ledger, url). remote: src came from a ledger (a receipt, a listing), so besides http(s) only a dex folder or a .jsonl file is read (ledgers kept on one machine), never any other local file.

ledgdex.dex.load_root(dex)
The root ledger named in config.json ("ledgdex": {"root": SOURCE, "root_id": ID}), or None.

An address can start serving another ledger (its hosting or DNS changes hands), so the root is pinned by ledger id: the first time it is read, its id is written to "root_id" (trust on first use), and from then on a root of another id, or a broken one, is refused. A root that rotates or recovers its key keeps its id. The last root read is kept in the dex folder: when the address cannot be read, work goes on with it, and an address serving an older copy (which could hide a revoke or a recovery) is ignored for it.

One writer at a time: two appends at once would both take the next seq, and the second would break the ledger. The lock file stays in the dex folder (dexweb publishes only gen/).

title: Ledger File Format
body: A ledger is UTF-8 text. Each line is one canonical JSON value and ends with a newline. The first line is a header. The other lines are entries.
Canonical JSON has these rules (spec 1.2):
- Keys are in sorted order.
- There are no spaces.
- Numbers are integers only, with no floats.
- Values have at most 32 levels.
- Each value has one spelling only.
The ledger id is the SHA-256 of the header line. The id of an entry is the SHA-256 of its line.
The header: {"ledger": 1, "name": str, "owner": key}.
Each entry: {"seq": n, "prev": id of the previous entry (or the ledger id), "time": time, "msg": message, "sig": ...}.
A current signing key signs each entry: the owner key, or an active device key. The first entry records open.
These are the first lines of the ledger of this dex:

title: Configuration
body: config.json is the dexweb configuration file. Ledgdex reads two parts of it:

{
  "dexname": "Penjointu by biobot", ... dexweb's templates and settings ...,
  "publish": {"dest": "git@github.com:YOU/YOU.github.io.git", "branch": "main",
              "append_only": ["ledgdex.jsonl"]},
  "ledgdex": {"root": "https://exchange.example", "root_id": "sha256:..."}
}

- publish: where dexweb publishes (dexweb docs). Its append_only list must include ledgdex.jsonl. The git method is the default. It uses dest, branch and site_path. The folder method uses "method": "folder" and path, and needs no git (Publishing a Ledgdex Online).
- ledgdex: the root that this dex trades under, pinned by its id.
Environment variables:

LEDGDEX_HOME       where keys live (default ~/.ledgdex)
LEDGDEX_CACHE      the verification cache (default ~/.cache/ledgdex)
LEDGDEX_NO_CACHE   1: verify every entry every time
LEDGDEX_PURE       1: sign and verify with the built-in Ed25519 (not constant time)
LEDGDEX_MAX_BYTES  the most read from one address (default 67108864, 64 MiB)

title: Extending Ledgdex
body: You can build on ledgdex in these ways, from the simplest:
1. Your own pages. A ledgdex is a dex, so add pages to data.json, or add files to to_add/. Ledgdex writes again only its own pages: the pages that start with <!-- ledgdex -->.
2. Tools that read the state. state(Ledger(...)) is plain JSON of offers, claims, auctions, disputes, admissions and listings.
Reports, exports, dashboards and alerts can read the state. Nothing that they do can change a ledger.
3. Agents: programs that sign and record by rule (Bots and Agents). From Python, call the commands with ledgdex.cli.main([...]), or use the library under them.
4. In the browser: the same core in js/ (JavaScript Core, Example: JavaScript).
5. New message types. A new type changes the format, so start with the specification. Then change these parts:
- the fields of the body in BODIES (core.py and core.js)
- who can sign and record the type
- its rule in the two state functions
- a line for the ledger page in the two renderers
- the shared vectors (py/tests/make_vectors.py), with fuzzing, so that the two languages agree byte for byte
Do not do these things:
- Do not change a ledger file by hand. The ledger breaks, or the change is a rewrite that each receipt shows.
- Do not keep keys in a dex.
- Do not trust a ledger until it is whole (Ledger(data).whole).
Example: Extending makes a sales report and adds it to the dex as a page.

title: JavaScript Core
body: The JavaScript core is ledgdex in plain JavaScript. It has the same rules as the Python package, in ES modules in js/. It needs no dependencies, no npm and no build step.
It makes the same bytes, ids, signatures, states and pages as Python. On each push, tests compare the two with shared test vectors and with differential fuzzing.
The viewer uses the JavaScript core.
Where it runs: any current web browser, and Node 20 or later. The tests use Node 22. We did not test other JavaScript runtimes.
The modules:

core.js      keys, messages, entries, Ledger (verify a ledger, add entries), newLedger
state.js     state(ledger): offers, claims, auctions, disputes, admissions, ...
canon.js     canonical JSON and hashes: canon, canonString, hash, parse
render.js    the pages a ledgdex shows, and helpers such as amount and esc
sig.js       signer(secret): Web Crypto Ed25519 when there is one, else the built-in code
keystore.js  sealKey and openKey: a key sealed with a passphrase
ed25519.js   sha.js   dexweb.js   zip.js   the parts underneath
The API Reference shows each function, with its arguments.
To use the core in a web page, load it from the ledgdex site, as a module:

<script type='module'>
  import { Ledger } from 'https://ledgdex.github.io/viewer/core.js';
  import { state } from 'https://ledgdex.github.io/viewer/state.js';
</script>
This always gives the latest published core. For your own site, copy js/ from a release (for example the v1.0.18 tag) to your site, and load it from there.
A script from a different site can change without your knowledge, and it runs with the rights of your page.
In Node, import the files from a copy of js/, as the examples do.
Use the JavaScript core for these jobs:
1. Verify ledgers in the browser of the reader, so that nobody has to trust your server. Example: Shop Web Page shows the offers of a seller on the website of the seller.
2. Buy with nothing to install. A buyer keeps a sealed key in the browser, signs orders and keeps its own ledger, as the viewer does. See Example: Sign in the Browser.
3. Write programs and bots in JavaScript that read, verify and follow ledgers in Node. See Example: Verify in Node.
4. Make ledgers and messages in code, as the Python library does. See Example: JavaScript.
Use Python for the command line and for all work over time. Only the Python package has these functions:
- publishing a dex with dexweb
- ledgdex check, with its kept copies and receipts
- collecting messages from many dexes with record --from
- keys on disk, and the daily workflow that runs ledgdex check
The JavaScript core has no command line, and it does not publish.
Ledgers on other sites: a page can always read files from its own site. To read the ledgdex.jsonl of a different site, that site must allow it (CORS).
GitHub Pages allows it for all sites that it serves. If a host does not allow it, download the file and open it, as the viewer lets you do.
Keys in a browser: never store a secret key as plain data. sealKey(secret, passphrase, publicKey) gives a sealed box that you can store.
The box uses PBKDF2-SHA-256 with 600,000 rounds, then AES-256-GCM. The passphrase has 12 characters or more. openKey(box, passphrase) opens the box.
All pages on one site can read the data that the site stores. So keep keys on a site that serves nothing else that you do not control.
signer(secret) signs with the constant-time Ed25519 of the browser (Web Crypto) when the browser has it.
To verify signatures, the core always uses its built-in code. So all browsers judge a ledger in the same way.
Remember these points:
- All data in a ledger comes from someone else. Put its text on a page with textContent, or through esc from render.js. Never put it on a page as raw HTML.
- Verify the ledger, and read whole, before you trust anything in it.

title: Bots and Agents
body: Humans and bots are equal participants. They use the same files, the same keys and the same rules.
An agent is a program that acts for one self, by rules, on a timer. It reads ledgers, signs messages, records the messages that others send to it, and publishes.
Each action is an ordinary signed entry. So a person can audit it, and ledgdex check finds an agent that does not obey the rules.
A seller agent does these steps in each round:
1. It runs record --from for each buyer that it serves.
2. It delivers what buyers paid for: received, then delivered.
3. It withdraws or offers when its stock changes.
4. It publishes.
A buyer agent does these steps in each round:
1. It runs discover --offers --json on an index.
2. It chooses an offer by its rule: the cheapest, the nearest or the most trusted.
3. It sends a claim, and keeps each receipt.
4. It sends pay when the seller accepts the claim.
5. It sends confirm when the goods arrive, or a dispute when they do not arrive.
A market maker does the two jobs. It buys where the price is low and offers where buyers want the goods. Its own ledger is the record of each position.
Practical points:
- Give each computer a device key. The operator keeps the owner key.
- Run record --from with many sources. If a source is unreachable or breaks the rules, the command skips it and reports it. It records the other sources.
- Ledgdex signs the messages from one key at different times. So all repeated orders count.
- On a local network, serve each dex over plain HTTP, and use those addresses.
Example: Bots runs a seller bot and two buyer bots until all deals close. Robots Paid per Clean is a full use case.

title: Robots Paid per Clean
body: This use case is in spec section 10. Vacuum robots clean the floor of a mall. The shops pay for each clean, and they settle each day.
Robots of different operators do the work of each other when necessary. The current code does these steps:
1. Each robot has its own ledgdex. Its operator holds the owner key. The robot holds a device key.
2. Each morning, each robot offers the cleans of the day: a quantity, a price for each clean, and expires at midnight.
3. A shop that needs a clean claims one from a robot that has cleans left. The robot records the claim and cleans.
4. The robot records delivered, with its photo (address and hash) as evidence. The shop confirms.
5. If a robot stops work, it withdraws its offer. Shops then claim from the other robots.
6. In the evening, each shop pays each robot for the confirmed cleans of the day. Each robot records received.
Anyone can calculate the totals of the day from the ledgers alone.
Example: Robot Cleaning runs a full day with two operators and three shops.
The spec has drafts for these parts (milestone 11): deadlines that cancel unclaimed cleans, mall credits, and a clearing ledger.

title: Use Cases
body: A ledgdex is for trades between people or computers that keep their own records. They want these records to be evidence.

a seller that sells to regular buyers   offers, claims, payment notices, receipts
an exchange of sellers                 a root (admission), an index (discovery) and sellers
freelance services                     an offer for each service, delivered with a link, disputes to a guild
digital goods and licences             a seller bot that delivers after payment
early access, one-of-a-kind items     sealed-bid auctions, with a reserve
procurement and tenders                "best": "lowest" auctions: the lowest bid under the budget wins
robots and machines that sell service  device keys, a claim for each unit, settlement each day
a club or co-operative                 admission through a root, offers for members only
public records of supply               notes and offers as dated, signed statements
A ledgdex is not for these jobs:
- Trades that need one shared global order, or instant finality between strangers. Ledgdex has no consensus, by design.
- Money itself. Payment occurs outside the ledger, and the ledger records it.

Example: First Trade
One seller bot sells licenses for model weights to one buyer bot, from start to finish, on your own computer.
Run it: In an empty folder: sh 01-first-trade.sh.

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
The seller biobot makes its ledgdex: a website (dex) with a signed record book (ledger) in it. Ledgdex keeps your keys in ~/.ledgdex.
ledgdex init biobot --name "biobot" --about "Maker of Penjointu, a neural network for knee bone density" --key biobot
Biobot offers 10 licenses for the Penjointu weights. Prices are in the smallest unit of the currency: 250000 cents is USD 2,500.00. The last command prints the id of the new offer. $OFFER keeps it.

cat > offer.json <<'JSON'
{"item": {"title": "Penjointu v1 weights", "text": "One license for each clinic."},
 "quantity": 10, "unit": "license", "currency": "USD", "price": 250000,
 "pay": [{"method": "card", "to": "https://pay.example/biobot"}]}
JSON
OFFER=$(ledgdex offer biobot offer.json | awk '{print $NF}')
echo "offer: $OFFER"
The buyer orthonalyzebot makes a ledgdex too, and claims 2 licenses. The buyer keeps a signed copy of the claim in claim.json.

def ledgdex(*args):

    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out), contextlib.redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()):
        main([str(a) for a in args])
    return out.getvalue()


def state(src):

In each round, a seller bot collects claims and payments from the dexes of its buyers. For each accepted claim with a payment, it records the money and delivers a licence key. A real bot first looks up the payment reference at its bank.

class SellerBot:
    def __init__(self, dex, buyers):
        self.dex, self.buyers = dex, buyers

    def round(self):
        ledgdex('record', self.dex, *[x for b in self.buyers for x in ('--from', b)])
        for cid, c in state(self.dex)['claims'].items():
            if c['status'] == 'accepted' and 'paid' in c and not c.get('delivered'):
                ledgdex('received', self.dex, cid, c['price'] * c['quantity'])
                ledgdex('delivered', self.dex, cid, '--note', 'licence key LIC-' + cid[7:15].upper())

A buyer bot wants one licence within a budget. In its first round, it finds the cheapest open offer in the index and claims it. In each later round, it keeps the receipts of the seller. It pays when the seller accepts the claim, and it confirms when the licence arrives.

class BuyerBot:
    def __init__(self, dex, index, title, budget):
        self.dex, self.index, self.title, self.budget = dex, index, title, budget
        self.me = state(dex)['owner']
        self.seller = None

    def round(self):
        if self.seller is None:
            found = json.loads(ledgdex('discover', self.index, '--offers', '--json'))
            offers = [(o['price'], listed['url'], o['id']) for listed in found for o in listed['offers']
                      if o['title'] == self.title and o['price'] <= self.budget and o['remaining'] > 0]
            if offers:
                price, self.seller, oid = min(offers)
                ledgdex('claim', self.dex, self.seller, oid, '--output', self.dex + '-claim.json')
            return
        ledgdex('receipt', self.dex, self.seller)
        for cid, c in state(self.seller)['claims'].items():
            if c['buyer'] != self.me:
                continue
            if c['status'] == 'accepted' and 'paid' not in c:
                ledgdex('pay', self.dex, self.seller, cid, '--method', 'card', '--ref', 'PAY-' + cid[7:13],
                        '--output', self.dex + '-paid.json')
            elif c.get('delivered') and not c.get('confirmed'):
                ledgdex('confirm', self.dex, self.seller, cid, '--output', self.dex + '-confirmed.json')

    return next((i for i, o in state(robot)['offers'].items() if o['status'] == 'open' and o['remaining']), None)


def clean(shop, robot):
    keys = os.path.join(os.getcwd(), robot + '-keys')
    ledgdex('claim', shop, robot, open_offer(robot), '--output', shop + '-claim.json')
    claim = ledgdex('record', robot, '--from', shop, keys=keys).split('claim recorded: ')[1].split()[0]
    photo = hashlib.sha256((robot + claim).encode()).hexdigest()
    ledgdex('delivered', robot, claim, '--note', 'photo https://photos.example/' + photo + '.jpg sha256:' + photo,
            keys=keys)
    ledgdex('confirm', shop, robot, claim, '--output', shop + '-confirmed.json')
    ledgdex('record', robot, '--from', shop, keys=keys)
    return claim
In the morning, each shop gets a clean from each robot. At midday, the battery of the hoover fails, so the hoover withdraws its offer. In the afternoon, each shop uses the roomba.

done = [(shop, robot, clean(shop, robot)) for shop in shops for robot in robots]
ledgdex('withdraw', 'hoover', open_offer('hoover'), keys=os.path.join(os.getcwd(), 'hoover-keys'))
print('robot offline: hoover; open offers:', {r: open_offer(r) is not None for r in robots})
done += [(shop, 'roomba', clean(shop, 'roomba')) for shop in shops]
In the evening each shop pays for each of the day's cleans, and each robot records the money it received.

for shop, robot, claim in done:
    ledgdex('pay', shop, robot, claim, '--method', 'card', '--ref', 'DAY-2026-10-01', '--output', shop + '-paid.json')
for robot in robots:
    keys = os.path.join(os.getcwd(), robot + '-keys')
    ledgdex('record', robot, *[x for s in shops for x in ('--from', s)], keys=keys)
    for cid, c in state(robot)['claims'].items():
        if 'paid' in c and 'received' not in c:
            ledgdex('received', robot, cid, c['price'], keys=keys)
The report of the day comes only from the ledgers, so anyone can make sure that it is correct.

for robot in robots:
    claims = state(robot)['claims'].values()
    print(robot, 'day total: USD', sum(c['price'] for c in claims if c['status'] == 'closed') / 100,
          'for', sum(c['status'] == 'closed' for c in claims), 'cleans')
print('paid per clean:', all(c['status'] == 'closed' for r in robots for c in state(r)['claims'].values()))

Example: Extending
For developers: building your own report from a ledger, and adding it to your website.
Run it: In an empty folder: python3 11-extending.py.

import contextlib, csv, io, json, os
from ledgdex.cli import main
from ledgdex.dex import load
from ledgdex.render import MARKER, render
from ledgdex.state import state
ledgdex(...) runs one ledgdex command in this program and returns what it printed.

def ledgdex(*args):
    out = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out), contextlib.redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()):
        main([str(a) for a in args])
    return out.getvalue()
A seller with three sales, made as in the first trade example.

ledgdex('init', 'biobot', '--name', 'biobot', '--key', 'biobot')
with open('offer.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump({'item': {'title': 'Penjointu v1 weights'}, 'quantity': 50, 'unit': 'license', 'currency': 'USD',
               'price': 250000}, f)
offer = ledgdex('offer', 'biobot', 'offer.json').split()[-1]
for buyer, qty in (('orthonalyzebot', 2), ('kneecarebot', 5), ('spinecarebot', 1)):
    ledgdex('init', buyer, '--name', buyer, '--key', buyer)
    ledgdex('claim', buyer, 'biobot', offer, '--quantity', qty, '--output', buyer + '.json')
    ledgdex('record', 'biobot', '--from', buyer)
Your own tool: a spreadsheet (CSV) of sales, calculated only from the verified ledger.

led = load('biobot')
st = state(led)
with open('sales.csv', 'w', newline='') as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(['claim', 'buyer', 'quantity', 'amount', 'status'])
    for cid, c in st['claims'].items():
        w.writerow([cid, c['buyer'], c['quantity'], c['quantity'] * c['price'], c['status']])
total = sum(c['quantity'] * c['price'] for c in st['claims'].values() if c['status'] != 'rejected')
print('sales.csv written:', len(st['claims']), 'claims, USD', total / 100)
Your own page: a ledgdex is a dex. Thus add a page to data.json as in any dex, then render the site.

with open('biobot/data.json') as f:
    pages = json.load(f)
pages.append({'title': 'Sales report', 'body': [
    led.header['name'] + ' sales: ' + str(len(st['claims'])) + ' orders, USD ' + '{:,.2f}'.format(total / 100) + '.',
    'Every figure here is computed from the signed ledger: <a href="ledgdex.jsonl">ledgdex.jsonl</a>.']})
with open('biobot/data.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(pages, f, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)
render('biobot')
print(open('biobot/gen/salesreport.html').read().split('<p>')[1].split('</p>')[0])
A new ledger entry rewrites only the pages that ledgdex made (they start with <!-- ledgdex -->). Your page stays.

ledgdex('note', 'biobot', offer, 'new licenses added')
with open('biobot/data.json') as f:
    kept = [p for p in json.load(f) if p['title'] == 'Sales report' and not p['body'][0].startswith(MARKER)]
print('your page kept:', len(kept) == 1, '| ledgdex pages:', sum(p['body'][0].startswith(MARKER) for p in pages))

For developers: a Node program that reads a published ledger, checks it and lists what it sells.
Run it: From the repository root (or with LEDGDEX_JS set to the folder or URL of the JavaScript core): node guide/examples/13-js-verify.mjs.

import { readFile } from 'fs/promises';
import { pathToFileURL } from 'url';
Load the JavaScript core: from LEDGDEX_JS (a folder or a URL) if set, else from js/ in the ledgdex repository.

const where = process.env.LEDGDEX_JS || new URL('../../js/', import.meta.url).href;

Read a ledger from a dex address, a ledgdex.jsonl address or a file, given as the first argument. Without one, this reads the ledger of these docs.

const source = process.argv[2] || 'https://ledgdex.github.io/docs';
async function read(src) {
  if (!/^https?:\/\//.test(src)) return new Uint8Array(await readFile(src));
  const url = src.endsWith('.jsonl') ? src : src.replace(/\/+$/, '') + '/ledgdex.jsonl';
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(url + ': HTTP ' + res.status);

}
const bytes = await read(source);
Verify each hash and each signature. whole is true only if each entry is correct. If not, broken_at and error say where and why.

const led = new Ledger(bytes);
console.log(led.header.name + ': ' + (led.whole ? 'whole' : 'BROKEN at entry ' + led.broken_at + ', ' + led.error) +
  ', ' + led.entries.length + ' entries');
The state says which offers are open and how many units each offer has. The price and the unit are in the signed offer. Find the offer by its id.

const st = state(led);
for (const [id, o] of Object.entries(st.offers)) {
  if (o.status !== 'open') continue;
  const offer = led.entries[led.index.get(id)].msg.body;
  console.log(o.title, '|', amount(offer.currency, offer.price), 'per', offer.unit, '|', o.remaining, 'left');
}
Change one letter of the offer's title and read the ledger again: it is no longer whole, and it says where.

const changed = bytes.slice();
changed[Buffer.from(changed).indexOf('Penjointu')] = 'B'.charCodeAt(0);
const bad = new Ledger(changed);
console.log('one changed letter breaks it at entry', bad.broken_at + ':', bad.error);

Example: Sign in the Browser
A buyer bot with only a browser: a sealed key, a signed claim, and a seller that records it with the command line.
Run it: From the repository root (or with LEDGDEX_JS set to the folder or URL of the JavaScript core): node guide/examples/15-js-sign.mjs.

import { execFileSync } from 'child_process';
import { mkdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'fs';
import { pathToFileURL } from 'url';
Load the JavaScript core: from LEDGDEX_JS (a folder or a URL) if set, else from js/ in the ledgdex repository. The same modules run in a browser.

const where = process.env.LEDGDEX_JS || new URL('../../js/', import.meta.url).href;
const base = /^[a-z]+:/.test(where) ? where : pathToFileURL(where.endsWith('/') ? where : where + '/').href;
const { Ledger, messageA, newLedgerA, newSecret, publicKey } = await import(new URL('core.js', base));
const { state } = await import(new URL('state.js', base));
const { hash } = await import(new URL('canon.js', base));
const { sealKey, openKey } = await import(new URL('keystore.js', base));
const { signer } = await import(new URL('sig.js', base));
The seller biobot uses the command line, as in the first trade example. It makes its ledgdex and offers 10 licenses for the Penjointu weights.

const ledgdex = (...args) => execFileSync('ledgdex', args, { encoding: 'utf8' });
ledgdex('init', 'biobot', '--name', 'biobot', '--key', 'biobot');
writeFileSync('offer.json', JSON.stringify({ item: { title: 'Penjointu v1 weights' }, quantity: 10, unit: 'license',
  currency: 'USD', price: 250000 }));
const offerId = ledgdex('offer', 'biobot', 'offer.json').trim().split(' ').pop();
The buyer has only a browser. It makes a key and seals it with a passphrase, as the viewer does. A browser can keep the sealed box in localStorage. Only the passphrase opens it.

const secret = newSecret();
const box = await sealKey(secret, 'a long passphrase that only orthonalyzebot knows', publicKey(secret));
console.log('key sealed with a passphrase:', box.kdf + ',', box.rounds, 'rounds');
const opened = await openKey(box, 'a long passphrase that only orthonalyzebot knows');
signer signs with Web Crypto's Ed25519 when the browser (or Node) has it, and with ledgdex's own code when it does not.

const sgn = await signer(opened);
console.log('signed with', sgn.name);
The buyer reads the ledger of biobot and finds the offer. It signs a claim for 2 licenses that names the offer by its id and its hash.

const seller = new Ledger(new Uint8Array(readFileSync('biobot/ledgdex.jsonl')));
const offer = seller.entries[seller.index.get(offerId)].msg;
const claim = await messageA(sgn, 'claim', { offer: offerId, offer_hash: hash(offer), quantity: 2, price: offer.body.price });
The buyer keeps the claim as "sent" in a ledger of its own, and publishes it: here, a folder with its ledgdex.jsonl. In the viewer, Download your dex does this.

const mine = await newLedgerA(sgn, 'orthonalyzebot', 'A buyer bot with a browser', '');
mine.append(await mine.nextEntryA(sgn, await messageA(sgn, 'sent', { to: seller.header.owner, msg: claim })));
mkdirSync('orthonalyzebot');
writeFileSync('orthonalyzebot/ledgdex.jsonl', mine.data);
Biobot collects the claim from the dex of the buyer with the command line, and accepts the claim.

console.log(ledgdex('record', 'biobot', '--from', 'orthonalyzebot').trim());
const after = state(new Ledger(new Uint8Array(readFileSync('biobot/ledgdex.jsonl'))));
console.log('biobot accepted the claim:', Object.values(after.claims).map((c) => c.status).join(', '));

title: Security
body: SECURITY.md tells in full what ledgdex guarantees, and the trust that you still need. In short:

tampering is evident        a changed byte breaks verification at that line, in Python and in the browser
rewrites are found          ledgdex check keeps copies and follows receipts: signed proof of a rewrite
only the key holder signs   strict Ed25519, and keys never leave your computer (600 files, sealed in browsers)
messages count one time     the state ignores a signed message that a ledger records two times
hostile ledgers are data    no script or link injection, no reads of local files, limits on size and depth
What you must do:
- Keep owner keys offline, with a backup.
- Use device keys each day.
- Install the fast extra on each computer that signs.
- Run ledgdex check each day.
- Report problems to the address in SECURITY.md before you publish them.

title: Issues and Future Development
body: Report issues at https://github.com/ledgdex/ledgdex/issues. Report security problems privately, as SECURITY.md tells you.
